tier_reason: The README tables (Ryzen 7 7800X3D, CachyOS, single thread) show White 1.67 GB/s and Orange 1.54 GB/s encode on silesia.tar versus lz4 --fast=20 at 0.98 and zstd --fast=5 at 0.69, and state the 1.6x / 2.5x geomeans; the harness is public (scripts/bench.fish, timing CLI runs with poop) but the lz4/zstd binaries are distro builds with no compiler or flags, so first-party C. The independent lzbench 2.4 row is for the predecessor skim 0.1.0 (2313 / 3500 MB/s, 64.53% versus lz4 --fast -17 at 924 / 3977 MB/s, 62.15%), not the current codec, so it does not lift the tier.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Firetrail built with Zig in release-fast mode (README: zig build bench --release=fast); the end-to-end tables come from scripts/bench.fish, which times the firetrail, zstd and lz4 CLIs with poop. Baseline zstd 1.5.7 and lz4 1.10.0 are system binaries with no build flags stated.
corrections.caveats: Baselines are non-default fast settings (lz4 --fast=20, zstd --fast=5), both -T1. White's figures use a 512 KB dictionary trained by Red on the very input being compressed and not counted in the output size, which flatters White's ratio and is not a deployable setup; Orange (cold, no dictionary) is the fair comparison. lz4 still decodes faster on every corpus (2.53 GB/s versus 1.89 GB/s White on silesia), and lz4 and zstd compress smaller on silesia and HDFS.log. enwik8 nearly fits the 96 MB L3, which the author says flatters it. No LICENSE file in the repo, so code must not be copied. The old skim repo only shows a migration notice pointing to Firetrail; the lzbench row is for skim 0.1.0, an earlier codec version.

notes: All README numbers match, including Orange ratio 1.54x versus lz4 1.56x on silesia. Repo: 1 star, 0 forks, 63 commits, no LICENSE file, last commit 2026-08-04; github.com/vantorrewannes/skim (3 stars) shows 'Skim migrated to Firetrail'.

tier_reason: The README says Gipfeli compresses at about 180 MB/s or more and decompresses at about 300 MB/s on a single core of a Core i7, 'typically 5x faster than zlib', with no workload, compiler, flags, CPU model or benchmark code: first-party numbers without methodology, so C. lzbench carries Gipfeli only in its unmaintained/security-issues list with no results row.

corrections.caveats: First-party README claim with no workload, compiler, flags or exact CPU; the README does not say whether the 5x refers to compression or decompression speed, and it concedes Gipfeli does not reach zlib's compression density. Archived by Google on 2022-07-27; last commit 2016-08-16. lzbench lists gipfeli 2016-07-13 under compressors with security issues or no maintenance, noting 'Decompression file mismatch when compiled with GCC 14.2 using -O3', so the code has a correctness problem on current compilers and lzbench publishes no numbers for it. COPYING grants BSD-3-Clause for all code; its note about CC-BY-3.0 and public-domain files refers to a testdata directory that is not in the repository.

notes: Numbers match the README. Usability corrected from mixed to copyable: the repo's top-level file list has no testdata directory, so every shipped file is under the BSD-3-Clause COPYING text. Repo: 119 stars, 19 forks, 22 commits, archived 2022-07-27.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: SPEC.md section 12 gives the full method for the README's numbers: public harness tools/benchmark.py, decoder built with GCC 14.2 at -O2 (AVX2 selected at run time), AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Linux 6.12, against liblzma 5.8.1 and zlib 1.3.1 on the same machine, best of 9 pinned to one core; the M4 Pro table uses tools/bench_apple.py, Apple clang 21 at -O2, against liblzma 5.8.3 on a corpus built by tools/make_corpus.py. Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated, so A, with the caveat that the x86 corpus (Apple OTA payloads) is not redistributable.

corrections.claimed_speedup: x86-64 (Ryzen 9 7950X, AVX2 path): decoder 1.96x xz -6 throughput per the README (SPEC.md section 12.4: 2182 versus 1096 MiB/s size-weighted, 1.99x; dense subset 1071 versus 642 MiB/s, 1.67x) on 89.7 MiB of real OS 27 OTA payloads, at ratio on par with xz -6 (10 wins, 9 losses, 1 tie; Apple's encoder produced the streams); decoder memory 35,336 bytes versus 8.06 MiB for liblzma at -6. Apple M4 Pro NEON path: 954 MiB/s versus xz -6 at 328 MiB/s (2.91x) on a substitute corpus.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2 at -O2 with run-time SIMD dispatch (avx2 selected) on x86-64; Apple clang 21 at -O2 on the M4 Pro; liblzma 5.8.1 and zlib 1.3.1 (x86) and liblzma 5.8.3 (M4 Pro) as baselines, their build flags not stated
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4), Linux 6.12, single pinned core for the x86 tables; Apple M4 Pro (10P + 4E), macOS 27.0 for the NEON table
corrections.caveats: Measured on a niche corpus of OS payloads that compress 29.9x; the ratio parity with xz -6 is for streams written by Apple's encoder, while this library's own encoder is about 4% larger than Apple's. On the dense subset zlib -6 decodes faster (1282 MiB/s) than liblzraven (1071 MiB/s), though at much lower ratio (8.85x versus 13.77x). The x86 corpus is carved from Apple OTA payloads and is not redistributable, so only the M4 Pro table (built with tools/make_corpus.py, which needs Apple's native encoder) can be reproduced from public data. The README admits Apple's own decoder is faster (1333 versus 954 MiB/s). The repo is entirely AI-authored and the owner says he does not intend to maintain it; one commit (2026-07-30). Compared against xz and zlib only, not zstd. The format has no integrity checks. TurboBench lists it as an Apple lzraven reimplementation.

notes: All README figures appear as stated; SPEC.md section 12 supplies the methodology the record lacked, hence the upgrade to A. Repo: 0BSD, 7 stars, 1 fork, a single commit dated 2026-07-30; tools/ holds benchmark.py, bench_apple.py and make_corpus.py.
